name: Pinealon

lead: Pinealon is a three-amino-acid peptide (glutamic acid, aspartic acid, arginine) developed in Russia as a brain-focused "bioregulator". It is promoted for neuroprotection and anti-aging, and its looks angle is better sleep, cognition and healthier aging.

Lab studies report that pinealon reduces reactive-oxygen-species build-up in cultured neurons and other cells and modulates signalling such as ERK 1/2, and labelled short peptides were reported to enter the cell nucleus and bind DNA in vitro. Published work is mostly cell cultures and rats, such as protection of rat offspring from prenatal hyperhomocysteinemia; a few Russian-language reports involve human groups.

paras: It is sold as a research peptide and used in nootropic and longevity routines, often in short courses. Effects people look for are subjective, such as sleep and mental clarity.
No systematic safety data are available. It is not an approved medicine and is sold as a research peptide.

angle.text: Pinealon is a short peptide marketed for brain and anti-aging use, with a looks angle through better sleep and healthier aging. Evidence is cell and rat data plus small Russian-language human reports.

lead: Pinealon is a synthetic tripeptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Arg (EDR) developed in Vladimir Khavinson's peptide bioregulator program. It is described as acting on the brain and nervous system, and it is discussed in nootropic and anti-aging circles.

Published research consists of cell-culture studies and rat experiments, such as protection of rat offspring from prenatal hyperhomocysteinemia [1] and reduced oxidative stress in cultured cells [2]. Russian-language reports describe human groups [3][4]. It is not an approved drug, and no link to facial appearance is documented.

paras: In cerebellar granule cells, neutrophils and PC12 cells, pinealon was reported to restrict accumulation of reactive oxygen species in a dose-dependent way and to reduce necrotic cell death, alongside delayed ERK 1/2 activation [2]. In rats, giving pinealon to pregnant animals with experimental hyperhomocysteinemia was reported to improve offspring spatial learning and make cerebellar neurons more resistant to oxidative stress [1]. A study with fluorescence-labelled peptides, including pinealon, found they entered HeLa cells and nuclei and interacted with DNA oligonucleotides in vitro [5]. A Russian-language review compares pinealon with other peptide neuroprotectants such as semax [6].

Evidence in humans is limited to Russian-language reports. One describes peptide-based correction of neurotic disorders in professional truck drivers [3]; another examines synthetic peptides in elderly patients with chronic polymorbidity and organic brain syndrome [4]. A review describes clinical applications of neuroprotective peptides in elderly people [6]. No randomized, independently replicated trial of pinealon was found.
No systematic safety data in the sources. Pinealon is not an approved medicine in the US or EU.
